name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_CYCLE_AND_CELL_DIVISION_MCQ_Q01 - Metabolic status of cells in quiescent phase

questiontext.text:
Refer to the given schematic diagram representing the phases of a eukaryotic cell cycle:

Some cells in adult animals exit the \(\text{G}_1\) phase to enter an inactive stage called the quiescent stage \((\text{G}_0)\). Which of the following statements correctly describes the cells in this stage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Conditions and Diagram Interpretation
The diagram illustrates the sequential progression of the eukaryotic cell cycle through interphase (\(\text{G}_1\), \(\text{S}\), \(\text{G}_2\)) and the division phase (\(\text{M}\) phase). An arrow branching from the \(\text{G}_1\) phase indicates the exit of cells into the quiescent stage \((\text{G}_0)\).

Step 2: Physiological Significance of the Quiescent Stage
Certain differentiated cells in adult animals, such as cardiac muscle cells and mature nerve cells, do not exhibit regular division. Other cell types divide only periodically to replace damaged or lost cells. When these cells do not undergo immediate division, they suspend the standard cycle and transition from the \(\text{G}_1\) phase into the quiescent stage \((\text{G}_0)\).

Step 3: Metabolic and Proliferative Characteristics
Cells residing in the \(\text{G}_0\) stage do not replicate their DNA or undergo division under normal circumstances. Crucially, they are neither necrotic nor metabolically dormant; they remain actively engaged in standard metabolism and cellular maintenance. They retain the capacity to re-enter the proliferative cycle when recruited by appropriate physiological triggers, such as wound healing or tissue regeneration.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Cells in the quiescent stage \((\text{G}_0)\) remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so depending on the requirement of the organism.

answer.text: They remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called on to do so.
They become metabolically inactive and cease all macromolecular synthesis permanently.
They undergo continuous rounds of DNA replication without entering karyokinesis.
They lose their plasma membrane integrity and undergo rapid apoptotic degradation.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_CYCLE_AND_CELL_DIVISION_MCQ_Q02 - Key events during mitotic anaphase stage

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates a specific stage of mitosis in an animal cell:

Which of the following events characterises this specific mitotic stage?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Identification of the Mitotic Stage
The provided diagram demonstrates the separation and polar migration of chromatids, identifying this stage as anaphase of mitosis.

Step 2: Centromere and Chromatid Dynamics
At the onset of anaphase, each chromosome aligned along the equatorial metaphase plate undergoes simultaneous splitting at its centromere. The two sister chromatids are released from one another and are henceforth referred to as daughter chromosomes of the future daughter nuclei.

Step 3: Mechanism and Orientation of Migration
Shortening of the kinetochore microtubules pulls the separated daughter chromosomes toward the respective centrosomal poles. During this transit, the centromere of each chromosome remains oriented toward the destination pole at the leading edge, while the chromosome arms trail behind.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The defining feature of this stage is that centromeres split simultaneously and sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles with their centromeres directed at the leading edge.

answer.text: Centromeres split simultaneously and sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles with their centromeres directed at the leading edge.
Chromosomes align along the equatorial metaphase plate with spindle fibres attached to kinetochores of both sister chromatids.
Chromosomes decondense at the spindle poles, losing their individuality as discrete elements while the nuclear envelope reforms.
Chromatin begins condensing into compact chromosomes while centrosomes move toward opposite poles radiating aster microtubules.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_CYCLE_AND_CELL_DIVISION_MCQ_Q03 - Segregation of chromosomes in meiotic anaphase

questiontext.text:
The diagram below illustrates the sequential stages of Meiosis I:

During Anaphase I of this meiotic division, which of the following events takes place?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Diagram Analysis and Stage Context
The diagram illustrates the sequential progression of Meiosis I through Prophase I, Metaphase I, Anaphase I, and Telophase I.

Step 2: Segregation Pattern during Anaphase I
During Metaphase I, bivalent chromosomes align on the equatorial plate with kinetochores of homologous pairs linked to microtubules from opposite poles. As Anaphase I commences, spindle microtubules shorten, pulling each homologous chromosome pair apart toward opposite spindle poles.

Step 3: Integrity of Centromeres and Sister Chromatids
Unlike in mitotic anaphase or anaphase II, no splitting of centromeres takes place during Anaphase I. Consequently, the two sister chromatids of each segregating chromosome remain held together at their centromere, ensuring that entire two-chromatid chromosomes migrate to opposite poles.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The primary event occurring during Anaphase I is the separation of homologous chromosomes while their sister chromatids remain associated at their centromeres.

answer.text: Homologous chromosomes separate from each other while sister chromatids remain joined at their centromeres.
Centromeres split simultaneously, allowing sister chromatids to migrate to opposite spindle poles.
Non-sister chromatids exchange genetic material through recombinase-mediated crossing over.
Homologous chromosome pairs align along the equatorial plane with microtubules attaching to both sister kinetochores.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_CELL_CYCLE_AND_CELL_DIVISION_MCQ_Q04 - Chromosome number and DNA content in meiosis

questiontext.text:
The diagram below shows the stages of Meiosis II:

Consider a diploid cell of an animal with \(2n = 16\) chromosomes and a DNA content of \(4\text{C}\) during the \(\text{G}_2\) phase prior to Meiosis I. What will be the number of chromosomes and the DNA content in a single cell at Metaphase II, and in each of the daughter cells formed at the completion of Telophase II?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Initial Cellular Parameters
The diploid somatic chromosome complement is \(2n = 16\). Following the \(\text{S}\) phase, DNA replication doubles the DNA content from \(2\text{C}\) to \(4\text{C}\), while the chromosome count remains \(16\), with each chromosome composed of two sister chromatids at the \(\text{G}_2\) phase preceding Meiosis I.

Step 2: Changes across Meiosis I
During Meiosis I (the reductional division), homologous chromosomes segregate into two daughter cells (dyad) without centromere cleavage. Therefore, at the conclusion of Meiosis I and cytokinesis:
- Chromosome number per daughter cell is halved: \(n = \frac{16}{2} = 8\).
- DNA content per daughter cell is halved: \(\frac{4\text{C}}{2} = 2\text{C}\).

Step 3: Status of a Single Cell at Metaphase II
The interkinesis stage between Meiosis I and Meiosis II lacks DNA replication. As the cell enters Meiosis II and aligns its chromosomes along the equatorial plate at Metaphase II, each individual cell retains \(8\) dyad chromosomes (\(n = 8\)) and a total DNA content of \(2\text{C}\).

Step 4: Changes across Anaphase II and Telophase II
During Anaphase II, centromeres split simultaneously, converting sister chromatids into individual daughter chromosomes moving to opposite poles. Telophase II and subsequent cytokinesis partition these chromatids evenly into four haploid cells (tetrad). Each resulting cell receives \(8\) single-chromatid chromosomes (\(n = 8\)), and the DNA content per cell is halved from \(2\text{C}\) to \(1\text{C}\).

Step 5: Final Conclusion
At Metaphase II, each single cell contains \(8\) chromosomes and \(2\text{C}\) DNA; at the completion of Telophase II, each formed daughter cell contains \(8\) chromosomes and \(1\text{C}\) DNA.

answer.text: At Metaphase II: \(8\) chromosomes and \(2\text{C}\) DNA; at completion of Telophase II: \(8\) chromosomes and \(1\text{C}\) DNA
At Metaphase II: \(16\) chromosomes and \(4\text{C}\) DNA; at completion of Telophase II: \(8\) chromosomes and \(2\text{C}\) DNA
At Metaphase II: \(8\) chromosomes and \(4\text{C}\) DNA; at completion of Telophase II: \(4\) chromosomes and \(1\text{C}\) DNA
At Metaphase II: \(16\) chromosomes and \(2\text{C}\) DNA; at completion of Telophase II: \(16\) chromosomes and \(1\text{C}\) DNA
